newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian newspaper speculates on oil firms merger.
newsitem.headline: Russian newspaper speculates on oil firms merger.

text.p: An elite group of Russian oil barons may be trying to create a new oil company by merging four energy firms, the liberal daily Izvestia said on Wednesday.

The newspaper, quoting "rumours in the upper ranks of government" and in the Fuel and Energy Ministry, said Rosneft (the state holding firm being privatised), Slavneft (the Russian-Belarussian joint venture), the Eastern Oil Company (Vostochnaya Neftyanaya Kompaniya) and Sibur (the Siberian-Urals Oil and Gas Chemicals Company) could merge.
Izvestia economics correspondent Mikhail Berger wrote that the new company, which he said might be called Nefteprom, would be the oil industry's equivalent of natural gas monopoly Gazprom GAZP.RTS.

But the comparison seemed meaningless, since other powerful, vertically-integrated oil firms, such as LUKoil LKOH.RTS, would remain and the new company would account for less than 13 percent of total Russian crude oil output at 1996 levels.
Gazprom, which produces nearly 100 percent of Russia's gas, also controls distribution. In the Russian oil sector, producers are separate from the Transneft state pipeline monopoly.
The new company would be 100 percent state owned for three years, Berger wrote.

Russia has created around a dozen oil companies in recent years, most of them vertically-integrated and privatised, as part of a sweeping restructuring of its oil industry designed to make it private, corporate and competitive.
The new oil group, based on 1996 individual results, would have a combined annual production of 36.5 million tonnes. That would be far below LUKoil's output of 58.3 million tonnes.
Izvestia said the four potential merger candidates sat on crude oil reserves of two billion tonnes but did not say to what extent they were commercially recoverable.
Berger's article appeared below a front-page story quoting an unnamed senior cabinet source as saying that a Kremlin reshuffle could concern even Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
The oil story ended with a challenge to the reader to guess who might head the new oil group, but quoted no sources.
Chernomyrdin was once the head of the gas industry and most foreign oil companies regard him as one of their guardian angels when negotiating energy deals.

Senior sources told Reuters in October 1996 that a proposal by former Fuel and Energy Minister Yuri Shafranik to create a mega oil corporation by merging four privatised oil companies had failed to find support in the cabinet.
